\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

A world model predicts how observations change in response to actions, so that an agent can evaluate candidate actions
before executing them. A growing line of work forecasts in the patch-feature space of a frozen self-supervised encoder
such as DINOv2 or V-JEPA~2, which gives compact models that plan without generating pixels
\citep{zhou2025dinowm,assran2025vjepa2,maes2026lewm,sobal2025pldm}.

Current latent world models are \emph{generative in feature space}: at every future step they regress the complete
grid of patch features, and most feed their own predictions back as inputs. In manipulation and surgical video,
however, most of the scene persists: the table, tissue, tools and the robot move, but they are rarely created or
destroyed. Regenerating persistent content causes three concrete problems. Static background must be rewritten
exactly, yet on held-out robot video every matched regression predictor we train is worse than simply copying the
last frame on static patches. Moving content must be synthesised as a displacement in feature space, which blurs object
boundaries. Recursive rollouts compound these errors: once rolled out, a DINO-WM-style predictor trained with teacher
forcing is worse than persistence on held-out robot video. Yet much of the future is already observed: on moving
patches of held-out DROID, copying the single best observed feature from a local window removes \geoOracleRed\% of the
error of staying put. Pixel and feature forecasters exploit such motion by
warping \citep{finn2016advection,liu2017voxelflow,saric2020warp}, but latent world models for planning do not.

We introduce \ours{}, a latent world model that forecasts by \emph{moving what it has already seen}
(\cref{fig:teaser,fig:method}). Instead of regressing the next feature grid, it predicts, for every future step, a
motion of the grids it has observed: each patch softly selects where its content comes from within a local window of
measured features, a gate decides whether it stays or moves, and a small correction adds what motion cannot explain.
The motion is conditioned on the causal prefix of future actions, and every horizon is decoded in parallel from
measured features, so predictions are never fed back. The transport weights, gate and correction are explicit tensors
that show where the model predicts motion, and because the design is an output head, it can be attached to published
world models.

Our evaluation suite has 18 evaluations across four axes (\cref{fig:benchmarks}): forecasting (DROID and its second
camera, BridgeData~V2, RT-1, Language-Table, IWS, seven Open-H surgical tasks), plug-in heads (V-JEPA 2-AC, DINO-WM
PushT and Wall), closed-loop planning (three suites) and five analyses. This version reports DROID, Language-Table, the
surgical tasks, the plug-ins and the analyses of \cref{sec:analysis}; the rest are marked pending.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
  \item We introduce \ours{}, a latent world model whose output is a learned soft local transport of frozen
  foundation-model patch features, conditioned on the action prefix, gated against the identity, corrected for new
  content and decoded in parallel for every horizon. It adds $<\!0.3\%$ parameters to a matched predictor (\cref{sec:method}).
  \item We demonstrate that \ours{} works as a plug-in head for published world models: it lowers V-JEPA 2-AC's forecast
  error by \vjepaMSERed\% with 0.16M added parameters under the same fine-tuning budget, and its gate opens to
  \vjepaGateTest--\vjepaGateEnd\%, so the large model routes most of its forecast through transport. It lowers
  DINO-WM's latent error by \dinowmPushtErrRed\% on PushT, but raises it by \dinowmWallErrInc\% on Wall (\cref{sec:plugin}).
  \item We show that under a simple motion model the MSE-optimal forecast is exactly a transport of observed features,
  which transport parameterises directly, whereas an additive head must synthesise the feature contrast along the motion, and we check the premise without a model (\cref{sec:theory,sec:analysis}).
  \item We set up an evaluation suite of 18 evaluations across four axes (forecasting, plug-in, planning, analysis), and
  demonstrate against predictors with the same encoder and architecture that \ours{} lowers held-out DROID error by
  \droidVsDirect\% relative to a direct and \droidVsAR\% relative to a recursive predictor, with small gains on seven
  surgical tasks (\hamlynVsDirect\%). It has both the lowest error and the highest action-ranking accuracy on DROID
  (\droidRankShift\% vs.\ \droidRankDirect\% for Direct), and is the only learned predictor below persistence on static
  DROID patches (\cref{sec:results}).
\end{itemize}
